Fig. 5.2 shows two hydrocarbon molecules.

![Diagram comparing hydrocarbon A, a straight-chain alkane with single C–C bonds, and hydrocarbon B, an alkene with one C=C double bond and H atoms](assets/001-diagram-comparing-hydrocarbon-a-a-straight-chain.png)

**Fig. 5.2**

(i) State the molecular formula of hydrocarbon A.

[1]

(ii) State which hydrocarbon is saturated.

Give a reason for your answer.

hydrocarbon ...............................................................................................

reason ..........................................................................................................

[1]

(iii) State the chemical test that is used to distinguish between hydrocarbon A and hydrocarbon B.

State the observation for each hydrocarbon.

test ..................................................................................

observation for hydrocarbon A ..........................................................................................

observation for hydrocarbon B ..........................................................................................

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) Molecular formula of hydrocarbon A: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Hydrocarbon A is saturated because all carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) Test: add aqueous bromine; hydrocarbon A stays orange, hydrocarbon B decolourises/turns colourless **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The bromine water test is the key way to distinguish saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons — decolourisation only happens with a C=C double bond, so alkanes never decolourise bromine water.
